body.head: Theatrical Examiner.
body.p: The new drama produced at this Theatre, called the House of Morville, is said in the play-bills to have been written "in humble imitation of the style and sentiments of the old English dramatists," and it answers well enough to its professions: it is an "imitation" of them, and an "humble" one; but though far from coming up to its originals, it deserves more notice in its humility than the grinning and vacant pretensions of our every-day scribblers. The scene is laid in England, at apparently an early period of its history; and the plot and characters are at first sight of a very old description. Lord Rodmund (Raymond) is in the ill-gotten possession of the estates of young Morville (De Camp) whose father is supposed to be dead and to have left them away from him on account of some youthful excesses. The young man, oppressed with debt and misfortune, seeing no way of supporting his wife, and believing himself under the malediction of his father, becomes almost distracted on visiting the scene of his early days; he leaves it in order to pour out his sorrows over his father's tomb; and approaching the cemetery where he supposes it to be, is forbidden the spot by a voice which intimates that the old man had been murdered, and by the very person who is now in possession of his wealth. Wound up to a pitch of agony, he returns to the mansion-house, and rushing into the presence of Lord Rodmund, proclaims him a murderer before his friends, but after throwing his enemy into great agitation, suddenly recollects that he has not sufficient proof to establish his charge upon the spot, and therefore goes madly forth again to discover it. Lord Rodmund, however, doubly anxious to get rid of so troublesome an intruder, takes advantage of his debts to bring the pursuit of the law upon him, and ultimately finding that his misfortunes have driven him to enlist, contrives to get him under the tyranny of a creature of his (Palmer) to whom he had given a commission. The Officer accordingly does his best to tease and gall him into insubordination, and in spite of the other's self-restraint succeeds so well or so unluckily, that at last, having added to blows the villainy of making love to his wife (Mrs. Edwin) he is forced into a combat with him and killed. Young Morville is now compelled to become a skulking fugitive, and having distractedly parted from his wife, the latter is rescued from perishing in the streets by an old gentleman, who is no less a person than Sir Thomas Morville, the father, but is unacquainted with her face; he is at this time living at a country mansion under another name and a sort of disguise, having been directed so to do by a Hermit, a friend of his (Mr. Holland) who knows all the circumstances of the parties, and had acted the supernatural voice at the cemetery. At this point of time she is recognized by an uncle of hers, who has just arrived from abroad, and who sets out with her in search of her husband, without any explanation, it seems, having taken place respecting the other relationships. Hearing a clash of arms in a wood, the Uncle leaves her in order to enquire into it, and lighting upon a wounded friend with a young man standing over him, concludes that the latter is an assassin, whereas it is one who has rescued him from a banditti, and no other than Young Morville himself, though his name is not discovered, till Mrs. Morville at sight of her husband rushes towards him. The Uncle, however, still supposes him guilty; and we are now conducted to the last scene, which is the solemn trial of the supposed offender, for the murder of his officer, before Lord Rodmund himself, who, notwithstanding the explanations presented in Court, is hastening to sentence him to death, when his Lordship's creatures appear against him, and his villainies are unmasked; the unknown Sir James, whom he had attempted to poison, and thought he had poisoned, ascends the judgment seat in his stead as true Magistrate of the district, and after the usual astonishments and congratulations, the piece concludes with the restored happiness of the House of Morville.

The reader will see much in this story that is of a commonplace cast, and he will find as much in the sentiments and language; neither indeed will he miss what he is pretty certain to discover in the dramatic productions of these times—an occasional want of good English, and an air of uneducated lameness in the general management of the composition. But still, there is in this House of Morville, with all its defects, one valuable feature, of which no traces are discernible in the general drama of the day; there is some appearance of reflection in it; the author does not always utter phrases that are in every body's mouth, nor content himself with pouring forth mere words; he handles an idea now and then with something like a tact; he analyses it, and tells us the result of his analysis: in a word, he is not destitute of thinking; and here is seen at once the difference of imitating those who do not think, and those who do. Had he taken the living dramatists for his model, he would have had nothing to do but to skim over a surface of nothings,-to repeat to us the cant of the day,—to be humorous by means of a suit of clothes, and to trust for success to an actor's grinning, or to some parrot character, who, as Jonson said of a person, "has but one idea, and that a wrong one;" but in resorting to the old dramatists, the first thing that struck him as requisite to their imitation, was to think,—to be conscious of a mind, —to pierce beyond surfaces and appendages, and shew us human minds in action, not mere human creatures in motion. The consequence was, that in spite of lame composition, of an ill-managed plot, and of a great quantity of commonplace, which seems to have always intruded when he had not his originals directly before him,—in spite too of an antiquated language which appeared ridiculous to the audience, the piece before us took strong hold of their attention. Nor was it destitute even of original character, comparatively speaking;—the tyrannical hireling of an Officer, who goads his inferior to distraction by continual and malicious exactions upon his patience, is a just and natural portrait, taken out of the existing and lasting exhibitions of life; and here again the author imitated the old dramatists in looking about for himself among his fellow-creatures, and having an eye to the real world, not in its external but its internal follies and sophistications. To select such models of imitation is in itself a considerable praise; and to use them as the author has done, without possessing, as I am told, the advantages of previous education and habits of taste, is still more. If he is advanced in life, he will probably obtain little further repute; but if he is young, or of such an age as to improve by what he reads, he may be of considerable service to the cause of the drama in assisting to give similar direction to the studies of others. The old dramatists are a treasure of sterling English,—an intellectual heap of things, —a fiery abundance of informing spirit. If they have any fault, indeed, more than another, it is that of thinking too much, or, if that is a wrong phrase, of giving you the idea of brains continually at work to an activity that amounts to a spiritual sort of punishment;—but they wrote in an age when it was the fashion to crowd every sentence with meaning, and a glorious fashion it was, though dangerous to a want of taste or to mere affectation. Taste, however, is now to be had in common; and after the Cobbs, Dibdins, and Reynoldses, nobody will quarrel, I believe, with those who should give us a little too much in the article of intelligence.
